summary: John Crepezzi introduces his work on Jane Street's AI assistant team, which maximizes LLM value across the firm. Jane Street's core challenge is that they use OCaml exclusively—a powerful but obscure functional language—for everything: web apps via js_of_ocaml, Vim plugins via vaml, and FPGA code via hardcaml. Off-the-shelf AI tools fail because models lack OCaml training data; Jane Street likely has more OCaml code internally than exists in the rest of the world combined. They also use custom infrastructure: their own build systems, code review system called iron, Mercurial instead of Git, and 67% of developers use Emacs. Inspired by Meta's Code Compose paper for Hack, they train custom models to generate multifile diffs (up to 100 lines) from natural language prompts that apply cleanly and likely typecheck. Training data must match the test shape: context, prompt, and diff. Features and commits proved unsuitable for data collection, so they developed workspace snapshotting—capturing developer state every 20 seconds with build status tracking. Green-to-Red-to-Green patterns indicate isolated changes; Red-to-Green captures error recovery. LLMs generate change descriptions filtered to human-like length. Training has two phases: supervised learning, then reinforcement learning using the Code Evaluation Service (CES), which pre-warms builds and validates that model-generated diffs keep builds green. Held-out RL data doubles as evaluation data: the model is given a problem, writes code, and the code is checked for correctness. Meaningful evaluations are critical—one separate code review model, trained on human examples, responded to its first review request with "I'll do it tomorrow." For editor integrations, they built Aid (AI Development Environment), a sidecar application on developer machines that handles prompt construction, context building, and build status. Thin editor-specific layers sit on top: VS Code gets a Copilot-like sidebar with multifile diff support, while Emacs uses a markdown buffer where users navigate naturally and key binds append content. Aid can be restarted independently of editors, pushing updates without requiring editor restarts. Its pluggable architecture enables swapping models, changing context strategies, adding new editors, incorporating domain-specific tools from different teams, and A/B testing (e.g., sending 50% of users to each model variant to compare acceptance rates). The team is also exploring RAG in editors, multi-agent workflows, and reasoning models, all built on the same pluggable foundation.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and OCaml at Jane Street
sections.summary: John Crepezzi introduces himself and the AI assistant team at Jane Street. He explains that Jane Street uses OCaml for everything—web apps via js_of_ocaml, Vim plugins via vaml, and FPGA code via hardcaml—making it a powerful but obscure functional language.

sections.title: Challenges with Off-the-Shelf Tools
sections.summary: Off-the-shelf AI tools fail for OCaml because models lack training data, Jane Street uses custom infrastructure (build systems, iron code review, Mercurial, 67% on Emacs), and they want flexibility to apply LLMs across the development workflow without system boundaries.

sections.title: Custom Model Training Approach
sections.summary: Inspired by Meta's Code Compose paper for Hack, they decided to fine-tune models. Their goal is generating multifile diffs (up to 100 lines) from prompts that apply cleanly and likely typecheck. Training data must match the test shape: context, prompt, diff.

sections.title: Training Data Collection
sections.summary: Features and commits proved unsuitable for training data. Instead, they use workspace snapshotting—capturing developer state every 20 seconds with build status tracking. Green-to-Red-to-Green patterns indicate isolated changes; Red-to-Green captures error recovery. LLMs generate descriptions filtered to human-like length.

sections.title: Reinforcement Learning and Evaluation
sections.summary: Reinforcement learning aligns model outputs with good code standards: parsing, typechecking, and passing tests. They built the Code Evaluation Service (CES) which pre-warms builds and has workers apply model diffs to check build status, enabling continuous model alignment over months.

sections.title: Evaluation Pitfalls and Training Challenges
sections.summary: Held-out RL data serves double duty as evaluation data: the model is given a problem, writes code, and correctness is checked. Meaningful evaluations are essential to prevent models from going off the rails. A separately trained code review model, fed human examples, responded to its first automated review with 'I'll do it tomorrow'—illustrating how training on human data can produce unhelpful but human-like behaviors.

sections.title: Editor Integrations and Aid Architecture
sections.summary: They built editor integrations with three goals: avoid writing the same logic three times across neovim, VS Code, and Emacs; maintain flexibility to swap models and prompting strategies; and collect real metrics on latency and diff acceptance. The solution is Aid (AI Development Environment), a sidecar application on developer machines that handles prompt construction, context building, and build status. Thin editor-specific layers sit on top. VS Code gets a Copilot-like sidebar supporting multifile diffs; Emacs uses a markdown buffer where users navigate naturally and key binds append content.

sections.title: Pluggability, A/B Testing, and Future Work
sections.summary: Aid's pluggable architecture allows swapping models, changing context building, adding new editors, and incorporating domain-specific tools from different teams. It enables A/B testing by routing 50% of users to different model variants and comparing acceptance rates. Aid can be restarted independently of editors, pushing updates everywhere. The team is also exploring RAG in editors, multi-agent workflows, and reasoning models, all built on the same pluggable foundation.
